en: Translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Master Xiang in Nanhai Commandery;
also titled *The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Resolving that All Dharmas are Like Illusions and Transformations*.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...

He was accompanied by five hundred great bhikṣus, including Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Ānanda, and Kātyāyana. These elders, who had long practiced their conduct and cultivation—having all cast off flaws and impurities to become pure, having planted various virtues over many lifetimes, and having accomplished what was to be done;

who were thoroughly weary of the body’s decay, understood the causes and conditions of consciousness, beheld the five realms as vessels of suffering and existence, and saw the various defilements of the outflows and afflictions; who took no pleasure in the three realms and constantly desired to renounce them.
Beholding all the cycles of transmigration, they contract their minds in awe and loathing; they sever and extinguish [craving], seeking emptiness with the resolve to reach Nirvana.
Abiding in that which has no returning, they dwell forever in that profound stillness and peace; they completely sever birth and death, exhausting the web of fetters;
being entirely free from all outflows, they have cast off the heavy burden and attained the four bases of psychic power, reaching the six supernormal knowledges.
They were able to abide in their physical lives, remaining regardless of life or death according to their resolve, having crossed to the other shore and dwelling in serene bliss.

Furthermore, they were accompanied by one thousand bodhisattvas—all of whom were venerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were in their final birth before buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), clad in the great armor of virtue, manifesting the renown of Buddhas, appearing as descending bodhisattvas, proclaiming the transformative teachings and disseminating the treasuries of all Buddhas;
their spiritual wisdom was exceptionally penetrating, they had already mastered holy insight, they dwelt equally in the Mahāyāna, and their resolve was like space.

By establishing the vast Dharma, he transcends the infinite; he is fully endowed with universal wisdom and clearly understands skillful means. He maintains all that is observed, encompassing the limitless, and his accumulated eloquence is immeasurable.

Following worldly conventions to guide others, he serves as a great bridge; his unsurpassed virtue and path are free from obstruction. He expounds upon the profound, infinite, and subtle, completely subduing the enmity of Māras and bringing all non-Buddhists under submission. He strides alone through the ten directions, circulating and returning at will; though he wanders through the five realms of existence, there is no coming or going.

Like the palaces of the sun and moon, or like a dream, an illusion, a transformation, a shadow, an echo, or a mirage, he is equal to these in having neither advance nor retreat; yet he moves all beings, delivering them across birth and death.
The transformation of the Three Jewels shall never be interrupted; the Way shall universally flourish and manifest, and all virtues shall be fully perfected.

Among them, each of the bodhisattvas had a name: namely, the Bodhisattva Youthful Ruru, Dragon-Head Bodhisattva, Wondrous-Head Bodhisattva, Great-Head Bodhisattva, Universal-Head Bodhisattva, Wisdom-Head Bodhisattva, Radiance-Head Bodhisattva, Sweet-Head Bodhisattva, Heroic-Head Bodhisattva, and Jewel-Head Bodhisattva. These bodhisattvas were present in a company of one thousand.

At that time, among those seated, the Bodhisattva Yingshou, receiving the Buddha’s divine intent, rose from his seat, adjusted his dharma robes with solemnity and performed the proper salutations. Baring his right shoulder and placing his right knee upon the ground, he knelt and addressed the Buddha:
“So be it, World-Honored One!”

The Youthful Manjusri is praised by all Buddhas of the past and present, by countless Tathagatas, and by the multitude of seers and sages who possess the way and supernormal powers; he is the one whom the Bodhisattvas who have accomplished great deeds in the past, future, and present cannot surpass, for he is the teacher of all.

He comprehends the profound and perceives the distant; his Way is deep and sublime. His brilliance surpasses the sun and moon, and his wisdom exceeds the rivers and seas. His penetration transcends empty space, and his eloquence is boundless. His virtue is manifest as unsurpassed, nurturing all through the four immeasurables; he benefits and brings peace through compassion, and provides relief through benevolence and magnanimity. His noble and vast virtue has no shore or limit; like a bottomless abyss, he dwells in serene and expansive concentration; like a formless body, he abides in tranquil stillness.

His majestic appearance is immeasurable; throughout the lands of the ten directions, he manifests the vast transformations of a Buddha. He is revered and honored by all bodhisattvas, and all Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings lead their retinues to pay him homage, look up to him with devotion, and respect him deeply. Among the hosts of devas, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, there are none who do not serve him; he is universally venerated and followed by the kings of the world.
The noble marks are fully perfected, and his radiant excellence is profound and serene.
As I gaze upon Mañjuśrī, he is endowed with all virtues; such manifold goodness is truly inconceivable.
"I vow to always sing praises and extol him boundlessly, lauding and admiring him so that his fame spreads throughout the ten directions, never flagging for even a hundred thousand kalpas.
At that time, Ruci said to Śrīśirṣa:
"What do you think, son of good family?"
"Does the Dharma-body have afflictions? He replied:
"That Dharma-body is without location and without form."
"Furthermore, the Dharma-body is entirely free from toil and weariness.
[The Buddha] asked:
"What do you mean, Viśeṣamati?"
"Does the Benevolent One understand the Dharma-body? He replied,
"As for the Dharma-body, how could it have a location, speech and sound, or traces?"
Furthermore, as for the Dharma-body, there is neither comprehension nor non-comprehension; it is like an echo or a shadow—how could there be anything to comprehend? He replied:
“To know that the Dharma-body is like an illusion, a transformation, or a shadow, with neither comprehension nor non-comprehension, and likewise beyond verbal expression.”
"And how does benevolence raise its voice to speak? He replied:
"What was said previously is like the sound of an echo; it is merely for the sake of explaining various texts to those who practice."
He said: "If it is as you, O Benevolent One, say, then that Dharma-body would possess interior and exterior, and would have this and that situated between them.
It would possess numerical observation; being already within the duality of numbers, it would then have a location."
He said again:
"O Chief of Excellence!

Regarding the Dharmakāya, there is neither resonance nor reflection; it is without mind and without intention, without thought and without consciousness, without speech and without discourse, and without difference or sameness."
There is no duality of destination, nor is there a single point of return; within the one, there is not even one, and thus there is no place of abiding.
This, O Chief of the Wise!
is the fundamental non-existence of a dharmakāya, the subtle and wondrous seal of teaching, the ultimate refuge of the world, the unsurpassed and peerless treasury of the essentials of the Path.
At that time, the Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
What Mañjuśrī has spoken accords with the teaching of the pure Dharma-body."

At that time, five hundred bhikṣus and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs in the assembly, having heard what Mañjuśrī had spoken, all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

Furthermore, two thousand laymen and laywomen of faith from the kingdom of Śrāvastī, who had not previously resolved their minds toward the practice of the Mahāyāna, immediately became firm in their resolve for the unsurpassed, right, and true path upon hearing this essential teaching.

Twelve thousand sons of heaven, their minds overflowing with joy, gave rise to the bodhicitta; each remaining in the void, they sang praises to Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī), whose accumulation of merit through kalpas has achieved immeasurable accomplishment.
At that time, the youthful Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, at the break of dawn, desired to enter the city for alms.
He donned the supreme, pure robes of a holy one, took up his alms bowl, and held his dharma staff, appearing roughly in accordance with the manner of a Buddha.

The mechanisms of his inspection and the regulations of his conduct were solemn; his gait was steady and composed, and his movements were dignified and upright. His every turn and glance possessed immeasurable radiance; his faculties were tranquil and ever-responsive to the concentration of the Path. His majestic deportment followed the descriptions of ritual law with strict precision; all virtues were fully present, and nothing was not elegant.

Like a fierce lion and like a great dragon king, his majestic fortune emerged resplendently from the grove; his majestic marks were immeasurable and his sublime features were extraordinary, his radiant countenance brilliant and his splendor luminous.
Just as Sudhana Kumārabhūta was stepping out of the gate of the Jetavana, he thought to himself:

"Now that I am entering Śrāvastī, there must surely be a multitude of Bodhisattvas from the lands of the ten directions who have come here; those moved by the holy intent [of the Buddha] should indeed act as if they were the Buddha himself."
Then, without moving from his place, he manifested emanated bodhisattvas from every single pore of his own body.
These emanations, surveying the ten directions, appeared as manifestations in all places; in each and every land, those who were transformed by these emanations each proclaimed:
"The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī bows his head to the World-Honored One and respectfully inquires after your well-being and dwelling."
"Is the Buddha’s reign secure and strong? Are his great blessings immeasurable?
Furthermore, the disciples attending each of those Tathāgatas were delighted and filled with joy;
they each asked their own Buddha, "From which direction has this one come to appear here?"
The World-Honored Ones of those lands each addressed their attendants, saying:
"There is a land named Sahā, where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

In that land there is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, whose wisdom of the Way is unfathomable and whose skillful eloquence is immeasurable; he extensively manifests Buddha-works throughout all kingdoms.

Now, in that realm, he is promoting and manifesting the Great Way; thus, by means of his bodily hair-mark, he displays his transformations and utters these words to move others and resolve their doubts.

The Bodhisattvas of all lands and all sentient beings, seeing these transformations and each hearing the Buddha’s words, had billions of kotis of bodhisattvas attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

The multitudes of ten billion beings, who were adrift in the flow of birth and death, upon hearing the name of Śrīmati and beholding his manifested response, all gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, true, and correct enlightenment.

The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions were without exception filled with joy, vowing to see Śrīmati and to hear and receive his pure, extraordinary, and sublime teachings—those subtle and wondrous manifestations of the Dharma—and to behold that Buddha and those Bodhisattvas.
The various gentlemen then followed countless bodhisattvas, each addressing the World-Honored One:
"We wish to go to the realm of endurance to behold the Buddha Śākyamuni, to pay him homage, serve him, and make offerings to him.
Furthermore, we wish to see Mañjuśrī and listen to his transformative teachings."
The Buddhas remained silent, thereby signifying their acceptance of the instruction.
Each, sustained by the power of the Sage, flew through the air to that land and suddenly ascended to the Sahā world, arriving where Mañjuśrī was.

All the Bodhisattvas who had come there were filled with reverence and admiration; some held celestial flowers, some carried luminous jewels, some grasped hanging pearls, some simply stood with palms joined, some performed celestial music, and some arrayed themselves in the void scattering flowers and powdered incense, blowing conchs and sounding jade ornaments. Others sang hymns in praise of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta’s manifest and universally beneficial supreme virtues. Some wished to escort and attend upon Mañjuśrī, proceeding with solemn reverence, gazing upon him without weariness.

At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, and the four world-protecting kings, along with the sons of the Sun and Moon deities, the various nāgas, and the spirits, each accompanied by their respective retinues, also suddenly arrived.
Śakra and the four kings shared this thought:

"Now, the youth Mañjuśrī, together with countless bodhisattvas and honored devas and humans, is about to enter Śrāvastī to manifest great spiritual transformations. We ought to transform the road leading toward Śrāvastī entirely, making it level and free of elevations or depressions."
On both sides of the path stood trees made of the seven precious substances; between each tree were seven jade maidens, each manifesting half her body to perform music and dance.

Their countenances were languid and alluring, their faces radiant with a brilliant hue, and their eyes like bright pearls—exquisitely beautiful and wondrous. With pure voices and elegant words, they sang of the Great Auspicious Fortune that moistens the head, and of the pure and sublime qualities of the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
As he stepped forward, he placed an incense burner and burned celestial *mākṣika* incense; various flowers were scattered there as an offering.

At that moment, on the left side of the path, all species of venomous and stinging insects—pythons, vipers, snakes, and scorpions—immediately had their poisonous vapors dissipated and withdrawn. Auspicious beasts and auspicious birds flocked together, gathering and soaring about in joy.
At that time, Mañjuśrī was surrounded and attended by hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and various devas and humans; he stood alone, majestic and dignified, with immeasurable radiance.
It was like the sun first rising over the peaks of a high mountain, or like the full moon amidst the multitude of stars, or like Mount Sumeru standing apart from all other mountains.
Like a fierce lion emerging from a deep forest, his radiant countenance blazed as he advanced forward.
Just as he approached the city gate and stepped upon its threshold, the entire realm shook and trembled.
At that moment, everyone was struck with awe; musical instruments everywhere began to sound spontaneously, and all exclaimed:
"What auspicious omen is this? What extraordinary and unprecedented response of a great portent!"
"Is this the manifestation felt when the Buddha enters the city?

Great and small throughout the entire kingdom were without exception filled with wonder and joy; their hearts were overflowing with delight and their reverence was immeasurable. Some ascended to the towers and pavilions, some climbed the walls, some peered through windows, and some stepped out through doors, all vying with one another in gladness as they turned toward the Buddha, hoping to behold his divine wonders.

At that time, King Prasenajit, together with his principal consort, his beautiful queen, eight thousand court ladies, and ten thousand sons, ministers, and attendants surrounding and escorting him, all harboring joy and delight, went out to welcome him.

In a mere moment, Rumaoshou suddenly arrived, escorted by a multitude of bodhisattvas and honored devas. He was endowed with the marks of a great man and fully possessed all the secondary characteristics; his golden countenance and sacred features brought joy to all who beheld him, and none failed to pay him homage first.
Among the assembled multitude, some scattered flowers, some burned exquisite incense, and some scattered garments and jewels.
With restrained minds and reverent intent, they gazed upon the Infinite One.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī proceeded forward into the city; all the venerable bodhisattvas and powerful devas followed him with solemnity as he turned his course, desiring to witness his spiritual transformations and to receive his instructions in the Way.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Nāgaśrī beheld the youthful Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta surrounded by an immeasurable multitude, proceeding with majestic and auspicious deportment as they entered the city together.
He said:
"O son of noble family! Where are you going?"
The Bodhisattva Niu-shou replied to Long-shou:

"I have just entered this city wishing to practice alms-gathering; it is out of great compassion and to broaden the benefit of wisdom that I do so. For the sake of rescuing all beings in the world—both devas and humans—I manifest the practice of alms-gathering for the purpose of crossing over through the meaning of the Dharma."
"It is because he universally acts as a great guide for all beings. Nāgaśrī asked: "How so, Vimalakīrti!"
“O Benevolent Honored One, have you not yet severed the thought of seeking alms?
He replied, “Noble son!”
I have severed [all attachments].

For one who practices alms-gathering while maintaining the perception of existence, yet reaches the state where there is neither perception nor severance, nor non-severance—this is called the pure alms-gathering of a bodhisattva.
Why is this so? Because, Nāgaśīrṣa,
all dharmas are neither severed nor unsevered, just as space is neither severed nor unsevered.
Speaking from this perspective, it is something that cannot be severed.
Throughout the entire world, including the realms of Māra and Brahmā, all the various assemblies, Brahmins, kings, and commoners—none of them are able to sever it.
Why is this so, Dragon Head?

Because all dharmas are like space: fundamentally non-existent, without arising or movement, without sustaining or obtaining; for emptiness is fundamentally without obtaining, without that which is sustained, and cannot be apprehended.

To state it briefly: all categories of beings, as well as other worldly phenomena and the various heterodox and miscellaneous arts of outsiders, are entirely non-existent; they cannot be maintained, cannot be attained, and cannot be acquired.
"All dharmas are thus: they are all unattainable and cannot be grasped, because they are fundamentally empty; therefore, they cannot be severed. "How is this so, O Mañjuśrī?"
“Should a bodhisattva mahāsattva act as an adversary to the various māras? He replied, “Nāgaśiras!
The Dharma is fundamentally without contention; one does not see a bodhisattva who would engage in battle with the māras.
If a bodhisattva were to treat the māras as enemies, giving rise to the perception of dharmas and engaging in contention, that bodhisattva would be terrified and cowardly.
Why is this so? Because that bodhisattva has personally given rise to fear and weakness.
For example, O Dragon Chief!
Just as a magician manifests transformations, yet that which is manifested by the magic is entirely devoid of fear or timidity;
so it is, Dragon Head!
This bodhisattva, understanding the dharma of fundamental emptiness and the practice of non-attachment, is without terror.
If there is a bodhisattva who experiences fear, that bodhisattva does not serve as the supreme field of merit for the world.
Because this bodhisattva does not understand the dharma of emptiness, they give rise to a mind of timidity and dread within themselves.
At that time, Nāgaśīrṣa asked Mañjuśrī,
“Can a bodhisattva attain the Way? He replied:
"A bodhisattva can attain the Way.
Nāgaśrī asked again: "How so, O Sūrata?"
"Who can attain the Way? He replied:
"One who is without name and without nature, without designation or title, without location, eternally without purposeful action, and without one who attains—such a person may reach the Way."
He asked: "How should a bodhisattva attain the Way? He replied:

“Nāgaśīrṣa! If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to attain the Way, they should do so without generating the thought of awakening, without mindfulness of the Way, without conceptualizing the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and without mindfulness of the realm of sentient beings. Their mind should be without location, without thought, and without attainment; it should also be without cognitive attachment. By means of a mind free from views, such is the practice of a bodhisattva, and they shall be able to reach the Way.”
He asked, "With what state of mind did you give rise to the aspiration for the Way? He replied:
“Nāgaśīrṣa! My mind is not manifold, nor is there anything that should arise;
furthermore, there is no initial arising, and there is neither arising nor non-arising.”

Furthermore, I likewise have not attained the Way; I do not contemplate the site of enlightenment nor sit beneath the Bodhi tree. I have neither realized the Way nor turned the wheel of Dharma, nor have I transformed those beings subject to birth and death.
Why is this so? Because, Nāgaśīrṣa,
since all dharmas are non-existent, they are without movement or agitation, without emergence or entry, and furthermore, they are without anything to be grasped.
"Because it is originally empty, I am able to attain the Way through this Dharma.
[Mañjuśrī] said:
"O Soft-headed One (Niu-shou)!"
This is the essential, unsurpassed, and incomparable supreme teaching.
Those who understand such a Dharma as this will be forever liberated from all afflictions;
and those already liberated from the multitude of afflictions shall, moreover, be eternally freed from Māra Pāpīyān.
He replied:
"It is not possible to be liberated from Māra Pāpīyan. Why is this so?"
This is because all Māras are also reckoned within the Way.

Why is this so? Because both Māras and the devas of Māra are fundamentally non-existent; they are without grasping and without attainment, without conceptualization and without thought. For this reason, it is said that Māras are also the Way.
He asked, "What is meant by 'the Way'? Niu-shou replied:
"O Dragon Head! The Way resides in all things, and all things are also the Way.

The image of the Way is like empty space; the essence of the Way is vast and expansive, stretching infinitely wide and broad, universally containing and encompassing all, reaching everywhere without limit or obstruction."
"Thus it is, Dragon Head!
The Way reaches all things, and all things are also the Way; this is called the unsurpassed true original state, which is itself no-way. He said:
"O Benevolent One, Dragon Head!
Do you wish to attain the Way? He replied:
"I wish to attain the Way that cannot be attained.
[The other] said,
"If you wish to attain the Way, is it not a matter of acting without frivolity?"
Why is this so? As Nāgaśīrṣa said:
"The Way that one wishes to obtain cannot be acquired."
"How could the Way be attainable?
If the Way were attainable, the Way would have a location.
It is like a person who gives rise to this thought and says:"
"If I were to cause a magical creation to sit beneath the tree of enlightenment and thereby attain perfect awakening—would such a statement not be like an echo?
For that magical creation cannot be apprehended; it neither joins with nor departs from all phenomena, nor does it have any attachment, because it is fundamentally empty."
If, Dragon Head!
all dharmas are like illusions and transformations, yet you give rise to the perception of existence and think to attain the Way—is this so?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said that all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, without thought, without perception, and without attachment.
Those who understand this have attained the Way.
All dharmas have no place of entry and cannot be destroyed; since dharmas neither join with nor separate from other dharmas, how much less could one dharma destroy another?
Dharmas neither conjoin nor disperse.
Why is this so? It is because, O Nāgaśiras!
All dharmas are without conjunction, for they are fundamentally non-existent and entirely without self.
Furthermore, they are like empty space: possessing nothing, without form, without thought, without movement, without agitation, and without playful activity.
All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; they are as tranquil and silent as space, like illusions and dreams, beyond all metaphor and comparison.
Since all dharmas are thus, they have no equal and possess no likeness whatsoever.

The assembled multitude, listening to the subtle and wondrous discourse of Mañjuśrī, leaped for joy and were filled with delight; each harbored no weariness, but with thirsty longing, awe, and reverence, they focused their minds to receive his teaching.

When this profound and wondrous Dharma of being like an illusion was preached, eighty thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression, and immeasurable devas and humans resolved their minds upon supreme enlightenment.
At that time, Śirīṣaka replied to Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
The Bodhisattva Tongzhen has eloquently expounded this profound and wondrous Dharma; it is truly unprecedented.
As I have now heard this essential teaching from you, I am enlightened for the first time today and consider myself to have attained the Way.
He replied:
"O son of noble family!
The Dharma is beyond speech and is neither seen nor heard; I do not speak of it as profound, nor do I speak of it as shallow."
The Benevolent One likewise does not attain it; the Way is neither attained nor unattained. Why is this so?
It is because of you, O Dragon-Head!
If one thinks of attaining the Way, is this not merely a conceptual play-ground?
The recipient falls into the view of having expectations, which leads them to say that there are dharmas of varying depth.
I have nothing to say; the Dharma is beyond verbal expression. It cannot be proclaimed, nor can it be practiced, for there is no one who can speak of the fundamental nature of all dharmas.
Furthermore, Nāgaśira,
it is like a person who says: "I am an illusion."
When he had explained the dharma of consciousness in detail,
the transformed being, who was actually without consciousness, asked, "Should one speak of consciousness?
Thereupon, that being gave rise to thoughts of weariness and contention.
Why is this so? Because those who have been transformed and lack consciousness cannot be the objects of discourse.
Thus it is, Dragon Head!
All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; they have no possession and no location.
Noble son, one who understands and realizes this is called a practitioner who is fully endowed with the Dharma.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Mind, whose spiritual power permeated his sight and hearing, perceived and heard Mañjuśrī expounding the discourse on the essential requirements for bodhisattvas in a different location. He suddenly arrived at that place and, seeing the great assembly, joyfully exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Why have all these noble beings, these great persons, gathered here in this assembly?
What is being discussed? Mañjuśrī replied: “Noble son!”
Within the profound and essential teachings of all Tathāgatas, one attains the name of a "Righteous Being" (samyaksaṃbuddha) and a "Great Being" (mahāsattva).
Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not speak of themselves, saying:
"I am a bodhisattva, a righteous being, a great being."
Those who harbor conceptual attachments and dwell among the ranks of those who engage in frivolous conduct, yet call themselves bodhisattvas and further refer to themselves as mahāsattvas, saying:
"I am a great expounder of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, Wondrous Mind!
Does that echo ever say, 'Sound has emerged'?
And does the echo possess an ear-consciousness that can be attached to?"
"In the case of an echo-like dharma, is there anything to be grasped or maintained?
Nāgaśrī replied, "There is none at all."
“Thus it is, Nāgaśīrṣa! All dharmas are like echoes, without name and without form.
Those who grasp at them engage in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because of this proliferation, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).”

If one does not long understand that all phenomena are fundamentally like echoes, then one will give rise to the perception of contention within birth and death; having given rise to such contentious conduct, one falls into agitation; and being in a state of agitation, there is no longer a flow through the five destinies of birth and death.
"This is simply because you do not understand its non-existence.
Thereupon, Ruci addressed Dragon-head, saying:
"Furthermore, son of good family!"
As the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus!
You should not practice with thoughts of attachment to play and pleasure; for you, I shall preach the practice of tranquility."

"Reflecting that the Lion of the Śākyas teaches the Dharma in this manner, one should listen and receive it with single-minded devotion, following the Dharma and entering into essential practice and patience, remaining free from attachment.

If a son of good family, as a bodhisattva, understands and accords with this teaching, comprehending that the fundamental nature is empty and pure, and clearly realizing such primordial stillness, he will be forever liberated from the destinies of the five realms."
Then Nāgaśīrṣa asked,
"Who is it that attains liberation from birth and death? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Noble son! What is meant by the Tathāgata’s transformation of birth and death into liberation?
Is there still going, coming, or the present?”
"If this is so, Dragon Head!
The Holy Teacher, possessing the ten powers, uses these essential words to transform and deliver beings from birth and death. He said:
"As the World-Honored One has constantly taught that all dharmas are like transformations, and as you, O Venerable One,
also say that all dharmas are non-existent, it follows from this that all sentient beings should surely attain the path of unsurpassed enlightenment?"
He replied: "Nāgaśīrṣa!
If all were to understand it in this way, this would be a discourse on the essential practice leading even to the Path."
Therefore, I do not preach the Dharma; the Dharma is without the thought of preaching, without receiving, without upholding, without gain, without loss, and without speech or words. Why is this so?
One regards all phenomena as having nothing to grasp, being without existence, without thought, and without consciousness, because they have no location.
Furthermore, if one understands that all things are like illusions, like transformations, and without any real existence, then all classes of sentient beings will reach the path of enlightenment.
For example, O Nāgaśiras, it is like a magical creation produced by a magician; yet the magician himself clearly understands the beginning and end of that creation, for he merely creates a creation.
Regarding all phenomena as well, there is nothing created, nor is there anything established.

Throughout the entire world—including gods, nāgas, spirits, and māras, as well as brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins—none, even reaching the furthest reaches of existence, can cause the illusionist to form a notion of solidity regarding that which he has conjured.

Why is this so? It is because that illusory person has personally realized that what is manifested is fundamentally nothing more than a transformation; there is neither illusion nor manifestation, and absolutely nothing exists.

Yet the one who creates the illusion clearly knows that all things are delusions produced by transformations, yet they give rise to the perception of existence regarding that which does not exist: they perceive the impermanent as permanent and the non-self as self. Clinging to thoughts of existence, they seek the state of non-existence; yearning for the formless, they dwell in nothingness. Because they do not understand the fundamental nature and fail to realize its emptiness, they continue to flow through the cycle of birth and death.

If there are those who clearly understand the fundamental nature of all phenomena, then that entire assembly will, within the Buddha-dharma, never turn back and shall attain perfect enlightenment. Why is this so?
Thus it is, Nāgaśīrṣa!

Because those sentient beings all abide within the reckoning of the Dharma of the path of awakening, they are all without obstruction regarding the Buddha-dharma; therefore, all sentient beings dwell entirely within the Buddha-dharma.

Yet sentient beings do not awaken to the fact that their own minds are fundamentally empty and pure: nameless, without consciousness, and without any place of abiding; free from conceptual proliferation, without dependence or attachment, and tranquil like space.
Furthermore, it does not nest within the unsurpassed tranquil concentration, nor is there anything produced therein, nor is there any dharma of a body.
Whoever possesses patience regarding the profound dharma of emptiness, such a person is never apart from the Buddha-dharma.

Why is this so? Because, Nāgaśīrṣa, the Dharma of all Buddhas can ultimately not be reached through conceptualization or mental activity. For anyone who harbors conceptual attachments, or who engages in verbal expression, discourse, proclamation, or exposition, it is absolutely impossible to attain the Dharma of the Buddha-way.
Thereupon, Nāgaśrī said to Śuddhimati:
"Excellent, excellent! You have so eloquently expounded the inconceivable Dharma."
"Who would believe that all sentient beings are not apart from the Buddha-dharma? Mañjuśrī replied, "Noble son!"

Those sons of the World-Honored One who are firmly established in faith and the Dharma—the ones on the eight stages of equality, as well as those who are *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, *anāgāmins*, *arhats*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and *avaivartika* bodhisattvas who are immovable—these bodhisattvas, who have already abided in the pure practice of the dharma of emptiness, are the ones who should believe this.
Why is this so? Nāgaśīrṣa,
those bodhisattvas who practice in such a manner make this vow to themselves:
"You shall surely succeed to the great enterprise!
When I ascend the Bodhi tree and sit cross-legged in meditative concentration, I will not move or shift until I have attained unsurpassed, equal, and perfect enlightenment."
"In the future, before all the devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts of this world, you shall become a great guide and let out the lion’s roar. Why is this?
If this is so, Nāgaśīrṣa!
A bodhisattva who fully realizes the dharmas of emptiness and signlessness abides like a door-sill; firm as Mount Sumeru, no one is able to move him.
Thus it is, Nāgaśīrṣa!
When a bodhisattva dwells in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, no sentient being is able to move them.
Furthermore, when this bodhisattva stands at the foot of the Bodhi tree and even at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they cannot be shaken.
He asked: "Niu-shou!
What is meant by the place of the Buddha-tree and the site of the Way?"
Niu-shou replied: "What do you mean, Dragon Head!
When you speak of the place where the Tathāgata manifests his transformations and the seat upon which he relies for those transformations?"
What is meant by the Tathāgata’s awakening through transformation and his manifestation of supernatural transformations to preach the Dharma?
Who is the Tathāgata? And who is it that performs the transformation?

The Dragon Chief replied, “I do not even perceive the transformation of the Tathāgata or the location of his Dharma-body; how much less could I perceive the majestic spiritual power manifested through further transformations, nor the teachings he proclaims or the emanations he produces?”
"All things are like transformations; they are originally non-existent and yet are transformations, and those transformations are themselves transformations—they are merely like transformations.
Mañjuśrī said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Nāgaśīrṣa Bodhisattva!

You have expounded for me the Dharma that should be observed with care; as one who speaks of such profound, wondrous, and unattached dharmas of patience, this is indeed the unsurpassed and incomparable teaching.
At that time, Nāgaśrī said to Mañjuśrī:
"Regarding this exposition of the essential Dharma of the wondrous image, there is neither the arousal of practice nor the entry into patience."
Why is this so? Because, O Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are fundamentally pure;
their characteristics are fundamentally empty; they have no location and no abode; they are without color and without form; all dharmas are entirely equal, like space.
"In this way, Śūra!

If there were any dharma that should give rise to the patience toward dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), then even a transformation of the Tathāgata would attain that patience toward dharmas; likewise, reflections, echoes, dreams, illusions, mirages, bubbles, foam, and plantain trees—all such things as these would also fully realize that patience toward dharmas."
Why is this so? Because the locus of patience is entirely empty, like space itself; there is no dharma whatsoever that arises as one who possesses patience.
Furthermore, patience itself does not arise, has not already arisen, will not arise in the future, and has not just now arisen.
Furthermore, this patience neither exists in this place, nor in that place, nor in any intermediate place.

This is the supreme, peerless, and essential patience; if a bodhisattva, regarding this mind of wisdom, is neither terrified, nor frightened, nor fearful, then this bodhisattva mahāsattva is indeed practicing the conduct of the supreme dharma-patience.

The bodhisattvas of supernatural power who had come from the ten directions, having heard what the Youthful Mañjuśrī (Rūṣu) had spoken—profound and subtle—all leaped for joy and attained this samādhi.
At that time, Rūṣu said to Nāgaśirṣa:
"What do you think, noble son?"
"Does that bodhisattva enter the patient acceptance of dharmas (dharmakṣānti) by means of unattached practice? He replied, "Mañjuśrī!"
If there is a bodhisattva who forms mental conceptions regarding their destination, they are acting with attachment;
they claim, "I understand the profound," saying, "I have deeply endured, am clear and enlightened, and I have already reached the Way."
"These words he spoke were all likewise attached to practice.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"By what practices does a bodhisattva cultivate that which corresponds to attaining the Way?"
He replied: "Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is ultimately nothing into which one enters; one does not think of phenomena, for one realizes that phenomena do not exist.
As for these phenomena, they depend upon causes and conditions; being empty from the very beginning, they result in non-existence."
A bodhisattva who practices in this way should accord with the patience of the Path.
To practice in such a manner is to have no practice at all; it is like a person sleeping and acting within a dream.
Longshou spoke again:
"However, as for that dreamer, he does not travel to any direction, nor does he go anywhere; there is no coming or going, no staying, and no sitting.
Once he has awakened from sleep, he realizes and believes:

the dream was an empty body, with nothing to grasp and nothing to abandon; it was entirely devoid of grasping, without form or characteristic, without location, and without any existence at all—just like empty space."
Thus it is, O Mañjuśrī!
The practice of a bodhisattva should be without attachment and without entry, just as space is fundamentally non-existent and devoid of conceptual proliferation.

This is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world; this is that which deserves all offerings, acting as an infinite guide. It is the most blessed ground and the practice of the supreme patience of the Dharma.
The entire assembled multitude, filled with joy and reverence, each scattered the flowers and jewels they had brought upon Mañjuśrī; gazing upon him, they were immeasurably uplifted and delighted.
Thereupon, Nāgaśrī said to Mañjuśrī, "We should enter the city together to beg for alms."

He said: "O Benevolent One, depart! When you go on your alms-round, do not think of lifting your feet or setting them down, nor of your treading. Do not think of movement; likewise, there should be no place, no dwelling, and no wandering. There should be no bending and no stretching, no mind and no thought, and no act of setting out. As you walk, let there be no conceptualization; do not conceive of cities, nor conceive of roads as you wander. Furthermore, have no thoughts of walled towns, districts, villages, or hamlets; have no thoughts of lanes or houses, no thoughts of gates or doors, no thoughts of men or women, and no thoughts of the young or the weak. Be entirely without mental activity; as you walk, you should be without thought. Why is this so? Because..."
Because their practice of the Dharma should be thus—there is no attachment, no form, no image, no arising, and no cessation; there are altogether no conceptualizations.
"One who practices in this manner accords with the unsurpassed alms-round of a bodhisattva; it is the practice of the essential path of purity and profound stillness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Nāgaśrī suddenly entered the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of the Ocean-like Concentration right where he stood.

The virtue of this samādhi is like the great ocean, serene and unchanging; it is tranquil, pure, and clear, possessing no other flavors. Its depths are profound and unfathomable, and within it there is no exquisite treasure or sublime jewel that is not present.

The ocean is vast and expansive, encompassing all in its great breadth; it contains and sustains all things with profound depth, magnificence, and vast serenity. Boundless and shoreless, its great waters are tranquil and full, where all virtuous divine dragons dwell, and upon which the massive bodies of sentient beings depend for their growth and development.
Thus it is, Nāgaśīrṣa! Those bodhisattvas, by means of the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is like the ocean, abide in essential principles that none can shake.

In this way, Nāgaśīrṣa, these bodhisattvas, through the ocean of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), contain all the jewels of the path, wisdom, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmas*). The ten directions rely upon them, and there are none who do not grow and flourish. Responding to the unsurpassed and subtle Dharma, they constitute the essential practice of being unshakable and beyond verbal expression.
"You should know that one who is thus worthy has attained the stage of non-regressive concentration and practice.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Mind (Miaoxin) sought to move the seat of the Great Being Dragon Head (Longshou), where he sat in the Samādhi of Ocean-like Wisdom (Haihui), yet despite exhausting all his supernatural powers, he could not move it at all.
At that time, this trichiliocosm shook violently in six ways throughout its entirety; yet the dragon’s head and body, as well as the place where he sat, remained completely unmoved.

Why is this so? Because that Dragon Head dwells without wavering; dwells without a location; dwells in non-existence; dwells without conceptualization; dwells without playful activity; dwells without toil or stillness; dwells without speech; and dwells in non-dwelling.
This is called the dwelling of the Way.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dragon Head (Nāgaśīrṣa) awakened from his concentration and, turning with reverence toward the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he rained down *kubjaka* flowers. Approaching the World-Honored One, he scattered them and praised him, saying:

"I take refuge in the Buddha, the God among Gods, who has caused all the bodhisattvas in this assembly, the multitudes gathered from the ten directions, the great beings (*mahāsattva*), the various honored great devas, nāgas, spirits, and gods, to hear such a Dharma—the unsurpassed essential teaching and the discourse on profound and wondrous wisdom. It is taught for the sake of non-attachment and being without a nest, because it accords with fundamental emptiness and stillness."
At that time, Miaoxin said to Longshou,
"Did you experience the sixfold trembling of the earth at the stage of awakening? He replied:

“Noble son! Whenever there is movement, one should perceive it as the shaking of the earth; the earth further rises and falls and quakes in the four directions solely because of that perception of movement or non-movement.”

Furthermore, even if all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas of non-retrogression throughout the ten directions were to cause the entire world to tremble, how could they possibly shake this most venerable place?

Observe the assembly of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas: although they have detached from movement, they do not yet realize fundamental emptiness; remaining on the ground of movement, they claim for themselves that they are free from movement.
One who has realized that all things are fundamentally non-existent remains forever unshakable regarding these phenomena, free from thought and attachment.
Thus, O Wondrous Mind!

By means of the pure essentials of the Dharma—the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—that Bodhisattva attains the state of being unshakable; he is then eternally tranquil, peaceful, and immovable.
He said again:
"Longshou! You may go on your alms-round."
He replied: "O Ruci!
I have now understood the supreme and most essential wisdom of alms-gathering."

Why is this so? It is because, having attained the state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) within the great ocean-like samādhi, one first attains self-illumination; thereby, one realizes the unsurpassed, equal, and true path of awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), manifests Buddha-works within birth and death, turns the wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings, and provides the stainless foundation for the causes and conditions of salvation.

Indeed, O Mañjuśrī! To have encountered you as I have is for me to have met with an unsurpassed spiritual friend; having been graced by your compassionate concern, my heart is filled with joy, and I am established in great virtue, comforted and illumined within myself.

"O Niu-shou! To me, you are the foremost of those who shelter and sustain; the foremost of those who transcend the great immeasurable; the foremost of those who are stainless, vast, universal, subtle, wondrous, and auspicious; and you should also be the foremost of those who are supreme and beyond discourse. I pray that you extend your five limbs to prostrate and reverently pay homage to the peerless, transcendent, and holy one, the foremost of the nectar of immortality."
Niu-shou replied: “Excellent, excellent! It is as you have said, O Dragon Chief!”
You have already realized that all phenomena are like a mirage, a dream, an illusion, a shadow, and an echo—devoid of name, devoid of form, and non-existent.

You should now attend this inconceivable sacrificial rite of the Unsurpassed Great Way; having attained the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and right reception (*samāpatti*) as vast as the ocean, you must act in accordance with this.

You should know that such individuals are in their final birth before Buddhahood; this is the eloquence and wisdom of a bodhisattva. Their attainment of such profound and subtle meditative dharmas—such as the ocean-like samādhi—is the transcendence of all conceptualizations.
He said, "If benevolence can be practiced, follow me for alms. Longshou replied:
"To emulate their virtue, one must practice benevolence alongside them.
Is it not fitting that these two sages should roam like dragons? Roushou said:

“I have no place of practice, nor do I come or go; furthermore, I have no advancing or halting, nor do I travel in company. I do not dwell, I do not sit, and likewise I do not walk. In walking, there is nowhere to which I arrive; in coming, there is no whence I originate. In dwelling, there is no place where I abide; in sitting, there is no basis upon which I rest; in walking, there is no destination toward which I tend.”

"O Dragon Chief! Suppose the Tathāgata were to manifest a transformation body—would that [body] have coming or going, sitting or rising, walking or wandering, lying down or sleeping, or waking from sleep?"
He said: "That which is transformed has no place at all for going, coming, sitting, or reclining.

"I am likewise with respect to all dharmas: there is neither abiding nor non-abiding; neither arising nor non-arising; neither that which has already arisen, nor that which arises midway, nor that which will arise, nor that which has just arisen."
The Dragon Chief replied:
"As you have said, this is an extreme teaching that is difficult for the world to believe.
Who would believe such essential wisdom as yours?"
He replied: "Nāgaśīrṣa!
Listen, O virtuous one;
would one raise up a lamp or a candle for the sake of those who have no eyes?"
Now, lighting a torch serves only to provide clear vision.

Likewise, this profound and subtle Dharma is intended precisely for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who are heading toward penetration and far-reaching realization; they alone are able to believe in and accept this essential path.

One who realizes such wisdom of ultimate importance understands that, fundamentally, there is no practitioner; such bodhisattvas are those who should purify themselves for the unsurpassed state and have long cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
These true sons of good family dwell deeply in the Dharma; they are those who believe in the Dharma, receive the Dharma, uphold the Dharma, and proclaim the Dharma.

Having turned the wheel of Dharma within the assembly of deer, they are worthy of the noble ones and are great teachers who bestow the eye of wisdom. Being those of immeasurable heroism and prowess, this is indeed the unsurpassed and most sublime Dharma.

When the youth Mañjuśrī had spoken these words, eighty thousand bodhisattvas within the entire great assembly all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Thereupon, the noble being Bodhisattva Suvicintita-mati, standing before the great assembly, leaped up with great joy; he cupped his hands full of jewels and, with a heart of profound reverence, scattered them toward the World-Honored One and also toward the youth Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Having finished the scattering, he joyfully and repeatedly sighed in praise, saying:

"I take refuge in all Buddhas, who have attained the noble penetration of wisdom; they dispel the mist and awaken those in slumber, shattering and dispersing the root of delusion; they resolve all inversions, release doubts, and remove the net of ignorance, entering the light of the Path in accordance with it to reach unsurpassed enlightenment."

I take refuge in the Dharma, the supreme among dharmas. Through the Dharma, many are saved and healed; it rescues those drowning in the mist of the dragon-like afflictions and washes away the myriad impurities of birth and death. It sweeps away the defilements of the mind and guides those who are deluded; the Dharma is unsurpassed, providing eternal deliverance for the ignorant and obscured.

Those bodhisattvas have long practiced the Brahma-conduct in unsurpassed purity; they are sages of celestial clarity and great supernormal powers, exponents of vast virtue, and members of the peerless assembly.
"In this regard, those multitudes who have attained faith and inclination toward these profound and wondrous dharmas now universally take refuge in them.
Mañjuśrī replied, "It is so, O Wondrous Mind!"
"Those who have no liberation shall, as a result, attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. He asked: "How so, O Mañjuśrī?"
"Who is it that has no liberation? He replied,
"Those who harbor attachments must seek liberation."
Thus it is, Wondrous Mind!
The Dharma is without grasping and without attachment.
Furthermore, son of good family!
All phenomena are entirely without liberation and without grasping; who then could possess liberation?
All phenomena are without bondage and without liberation, without holding, without taking up, and without discarding.
It is like a person saying to a magician:
"Good man! For one who has deeply entered the liberation that is to be grasped by understanding," the illusory person replied.
"I am neither male nor an ordinary person; I possess nothing, so what is there to be liberated? This, O Wondrous Mind!
The Way has neither grasping nor liberation;
one should contemplate its non-existence, for its very non-existence is fundamentally empty and pure.

In the *Buddhabhāṣita-lalita-vistara-bodhisattva-anuttara-viśuddha-piṇḍapāta-sūtra*, Volume Upper and Volume Lower, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Xianggong in Nanhai Commandery: At that time, the Bodhisattva Dragon Head said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, "Depart, son of good family!"
"I am going east to beg for alms. He replied,
"Dragon Head!..."
"Do these illusions and mirages have east, west, south, or north?
He replied, "I cannot even speak of them before you, much less dare to say anything about them."
Why is this so? It is because all these eloquent arguments have proceeded from what was asked by Your Reverence.
You, O Benevolent One, have responded in accordance with the Dharma, resolving each point without obstruction; therefore, I have no words and know not how to reply.
He replied: "The one who has attained realization possesses no words at all from which to grasp; how much less would he have anything further to say?
This is because all dharmas are without cause."
He asked: "What is meant by the non-existence of all phenomena? He replied:
"Dragon Head! That which is 'nothing that is not' refers to the non-existence of all these phenomena; this is the essential principle of all phenomena.
It is by means of this wisdom that one is able to penetrate those various sounds."
"To have nothing proclaimed is the essential meaning; is this not indeed the teaching on the ultimate essential meaning?
He replied, "This is for practitioners who continue to dwell within conceptualization."
He asked: "What practice should one undertake to be free from all conceptualizations? He replied:

"Nāgaśīrṣa! A bodhisattva does not form perceptions regarding the elements of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; furthermore, they do not engage with the fundamental nature of phenomena (dharmatā), nor do they engage with that which is fundamentally non-existent. By practicing in this way, they become free from all perceptions."
When this profound and subtle Dharma was being preached, five thousand bodhisattvas attained this wisdom, and two thousand devas and humans resolved their minds on Bodhi.
Then Nāgaśīrṣa said: "I shall now depart!"
"Because one who is in the state of a youthful truth-seeker is not my companion. Mañjuśrī replied,
"I have neither coming nor going, nor do I have a companion, nor am I accompanied by anything."
Why is this so? It is because the Way has no companion; thus, one does not even conceive of companionship with all dharmas, nor does one take the practice of desire as a companion.
Within the fundamental non-existence of dharmas, one neither perceives a companion nor associates with that which coexists.

Furthermore, as for "original non-existence," it refers to the total absence of any assertion of a self-nature (*ātman*), a person (*pudgala*), a life-span (*jīva*), or the phenomena of bodily sustenance.
It also includes the verbal designations of persons and things, that upon which consciousness and perception rely and cling, as well as the activities and pursuits performed therein.
The root of all phenomena is fundamentally non-existent in this way; with whom, then, could it be associated?
That which has an associate is merely a desire for association.
For example, O Nāgaśīrṣa, suppose there were a person of clear understanding who thought to himself:
"That which is emanated by the Tathāgata and that which is emanated by a magician— these emanations are equal, one and no different."
When these people were transformed, each of them said:
"I am your companion; you and I are together.
Thus it was, O benevolent One—O Dragon Head!
"What do you think? Has this person been transformed into one who has a companion?
He replied to Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī):
"An emanation has no companion.
Why is this? Because an emanation is fundamentally non-existent, it is nothingness, it is without form or image, and it cannot be apprehended."
He replied: "In this way, Nāgaśīrṣa!
Within saṃsāra, there is ultimately no companion at all, nor is there anything with which one is joined."
Where there is the notion of a companion, there is separation.
If one gives rise to the thought of a companion, this is already associated with desire.
An enlightened Bodhisattva should understand and dissolve the notion of a companion.
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, having neither companion nor non-companion.
Deceptive indeed are all phenomena—fleeting and unreliable—like dreams, shadows, and echoes; all that exists is like space.
Perception and consciousness are without stability; they have no location, no support, and no intentionality; they are without thought and without anything possessed.
Having already departed from all thoughts, one is without thought within thought, in accordance with the original state of non-thought.
He asked: "Rushou!
Have you ever engaged in conversation, walking, coming, sitting, or rising with an illusory person created by a magician? Furthermore, have you ever held discussions or deliberations with them?"
Niu-shou replied, “I do not see it. Long-shou said:
"What is the appearance of this illusory person? He replied:
"That which is illusory resembles the likeness of a human being; the transformed image produced by illusion is likewise such, for it is merely a composite image."
Why is this so? Just as it is with a magical illusion, it is neither liberated from that nor liberated from this.
The magical illusion is not different from the person, and the person is not different from the magical illusion; the person is precisely the magical illusion.
"Just as one who is like a magical illusion asks about illusory matters by means of the dharma of magical illusion, so too are all phenomena.
He asked again: "Mañjuśrī!"
"O Benevolent One, have you ever sat or risen together with an illusory transformation, engaged in conversation, socialized, held discussions, or dwelt face-to-face with one?
He replied, "How could that be, Dragon Head?"
Is there any difference between an illusory being and a transformation, and the realm of desire?
Is there any difference regarding the self, the person, the life-span, or the principle of nourishment?

By means of this discourse on illusion and transformation, I wish to question you, O Benevolent One, to see whether you, Great Being, possess exceptional eloquence in this matter; what Dharma would you then expound?
He said: "Your kindness is as you have tested; you merely wished to test the illusory and transformative nature of empty space.
You then conceived of this transformation as being characterized by perception."
“An illusion is fundamentally non-existent; it is without thought or reflection, without form or appearance, and without anything at all, for it is already free from all mental conceptions.
Niu-shou said: “If this is so, Long-shou!”
"The Dharma is also like an illusion; illusions are fundamentally empty, and this emptiness is formless and invisible.
[Nāgārjuna] said:
"O Namaso! (Rushou)!"
"All dharmas are formless and thus cannot be seen, is that not so?
According to what you have said, how should all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas receive their investiture and consecration so as to achieve the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment?"
"For whom was the knowledge of deliverance bestowed and the investiture performed? Niu-shou replied,
"What do you mean, Long-shou?"
Once, while traveling through the mountains, you heard an echo. Was that echo produced from within the mountains?
Does that sound have a place where it dwells?
And by what auditory consciousness was that sound heard?
Does that sound say anything?
Is there anyone who can grasp or maintain an echo?
Furthermore, who hears the echo together with whom?
The Bodhisattva Nāgaśrī replied,
“There is none. Viśeṣacintin said:
"In this way, if a bodhisattva understands that all phenomena are like echoes and empty, then all sounds are like echoes and are detached from those various voices.
Those bodhisattvas, by means of this, receive the consecration for the unsurpassed, right, and true path; yet herein, there is no one who receives the consecration."
The great assembly of Bodhisattvas gathered from the ten directions, having all heard what the youth Mañjuśrī had spoken, were without exception filled with boundless joy,
leaping for gladness, and singing praises. At that time, Nāgaśrī said to Mañjuśrī,
"It is now the proper time for us to travel together into the city to beg for alms."
"When I consider the time and date, could it be that I have transgressed? He replied,
"Dragon Head!"
All phenomena are neither in error nor do they exist at any time.
Those who dwell within the sphere of conceptualization and mental formations merely harbor notions of "time" and "non-time.
For a Bodhisattva who has attained clear realization that all things are fundamentally non-existent and who understands the dharma of emptiness, how could there be any talk of "time" or "non-time"?
As for all other dharmas, whether they occur at a specific time or not, there is no "time" or "non-time" that accords with the unsurpassed Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha.
As for those who rely on calculation to reckon time and seasons, this involves the conceptualization of "transgression" and "time."

Just as the World-Honored Ones and their noble disciples are always self-sufficient through the wisdom of the Way, possessing a wisdom free from conceptualization and cognition; regarding both the conceptual and the non-conceptual, they act without any volitional effort, and are without thought or even the absence of thought.
By means of this wisdom, they are perpetually satiated; the noble assembly of the World-Honored One has no thought of food, nor do they again conceive of the matter of eating.

To eat in such a manner as this is what is called the "noble and holy food free from admixture. If one forever partakes of such food, then one is eternally expounding the nectar-like food of the Dharma.
By the power of consuming these foods, he is able to sustain his life for one kalpa or even beyond a kalpa. Why is this?

Because such a person has already awakened to the nature of all phenomena; being entirely free from conceptualization, they understand emptiness and purity. Having realized this, they no longer possess the consciousness that seeks food, unlike ordinary people who have not yet attained such realization.

Furthermore, the Tathāgatas of Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment, as well as the sages and worthies of the entire world, possess the great minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; they bestow benevolence and affection, taking pity upon sentient beings so that they may arise in the world.

It is solely because they desire to deliver those suffering in the five realms of existence that these holy ones manifest entry into commanderies, kingdoms, counties, towns, and villages to practice alms-gathering; yet these sages have already transcended all forms of food and do not consume food, being perpetually satisfied by wisdom, liberation, and the meditative attainments of samādhi.
As for those who consume various foods and continue to eat, they undergo the cycle of existence and repeatedly pass through birth and death.
For this reason, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have full and clear understanding regarding all forms of food, and they no longer harbor any conceptualization of "various foods."
With generous and profound sighs, they dwell in peace and harmony; their number can exceed that of the sands of the Ganges.
From the first moment they resolve their minds, they shall forever be free from all hunger, thirst, and miscellaneous distracting thoughts.

When he reached the Bodhi tree at the time the morning star appeared, regarding all that he had received as food from the beginning, it was by means of this food that he—being a true person, a great man, a hero, a Nāga-mighty one, furthermore a lion, a disciplined gentleman, a multitude of virtuous men, a true person, an eminent one, various lotuses, a man, a supreme being, a charioteer of the Dharma, and a teacher of gods and humans—attained all that should be attained, all that should be clearly understood, and all that should be realized; having fully realized and perfected these, equalizing them as a single image and uniting his wisdom, he achieved the aspiration for the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Therefore, Nāgaśīrṣa!

All Bodhisattvas, as well as all Tathāgatas and the assembly of worthies and sages, rely solely on this food to attain the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; they are thus able to abide for a lifespan as long as the sands of the Ganges, or even many times more than that, while the Tathāgatas themselves remain forever free from weariness.
Why is this? Because it accords with the food of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*).

It is without mindfulness or non-mindfulness, without conjunction or disjunction; nor does it conceive of conjoining with the conduct of the noble ones (*ārya*). It is constantly in accordance [with reality], emitting various fragrances, naturally pure, without thought or recollection, devoid of all nests and lairs, and free from playful activity; it is fundamentally empty and inherently pure.
"In this way, Nāgaśīrṣa, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should partake of food; only then does it constitute food that accords with the Dharma.
Nāgaśīrṣa replied:
“Excellent, excellent!
The subtle and wondrous Dharma taught by Niu-shou has already satisfied me with this supreme food.

Merely hearing this essential exposition of the Dharma-food is already more than sufficient; how much more so for one who partakes of the long-lasting food that is free from defilement—would such a person ever again desire to eat or crave food?”
“Nāgaśiras, how could the essence of space ever have the consumption of mixed food, or even speak of being satiated?”
He replied, "Rushou! Emptiness is non-existent."
He said again: "Dragon Head!
Are you able to satisfy the phantom being created by the illusionist?"
He replied, “No. [The Buddha asked,] “How so, Nāgaśīrṣa?”
"Can one truly manifest an image within a stomach that is full of food? He replied, "No."
He spoke again: "Longshou!
Does the great ocean ever become satiated by the many streams that flow into it?"
He replied, "No. Mañjuśrī spoke again:
“Thus it is, Nāgaśīrṣa!
All dharmas are insatiable, like empty space.
Yet you have just said that you have the notion of satiety; how can this be?”

All dharmas are like space: without perception, without aspiration, without arising, and without activity; they are neither created nor produced, eternally free from desire, characterized by concentration and liberation; they are formless and imageless, lacking solidity or firmness, understood to be like empty space, and entirely devoid of anything to be grasped.
"All phenomena are thus; how can one conceive of satiety?
Nāgaśrī spoke again: "If this is so, O Suvikrānta!"
"If there are those who practice in this way, do they no longer eat any food at all?
And does the Venerable One teach that the nature of food is fundamentally empty? Niu-shou replied:
"If it were so, Nāgaśīrṣa, then all sentient beings would have no food. For example, Nāgaśīrṣa— "
“The World-Honored One transforms beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and provides food for these transformed beings.
What do you think, noble son?
By what does those transformed beings take their nourishment?”
"Is there, furthermore, anyone who eats?
He replied, "A transformation being has no thought and no cognition; it possesses nothing, and likewise has no food."
"How much less can one say that there will be food?
"In this way, Nāgaśīrṣa! All dharmas, whether visible or invisible, are like illusions and transformations."
All sentient beings do not understand this; because they do not understand it, they immediately transmigrate and undergo birth and death.
When one observes within this, there is nothing whatsoever, there is nothing to be attained, and there is no transmigration.
To understand that birth and death are no different from original non-existence is to have no further grasping, and thus no birth and death.
Failing to realize original emptiness, there is birth and death.
That which is called birth-and-death is itself without birth-and-death; within that birth-and-death there is nothing received and nothing attained. What, then, is the phenomenon of birth-and-death?
He replied: "Mañjuśrī! These words are most excellent."
"You should know that the time has come; we may go together.
Upon returning to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, our hunger and thirst shall be forever severed. He replied:
“Nāgaśīrṣa! It is like a person conjured by a magician who says, ‘I am hungry and thirsty. Is this truly hunger?
It is the nature of a mirage!”
Thus it is, Nāgaśīrṣa!
All things are like this.
These various dharmas are all like a mirage; to understand this is to understand.
And yet, would a son of good family say:
"I have severed my hunger and thirst"?
When eating this food, one eats as if eating the food of all dharmas: it is neither interrupted nor destroyed, and there is no hunger or thirst, for all dharmas are fundamentally satiated.
Therefore, those ordinary persons of inferior capacity do not understand this fundamental nature; they say, "I am hungry" or "I am thirsty," and yet they also speak of being satiated.

Just as the noble ones understand the fundamental nature of all phenomena, they have neither hunger nor thirst, nor do they have the notion of satiety; they understand all hunger and thirst, yet there is no birth-and-death, no frivolous activity, and no conceptualization. They are already unmoving and free from attachment.
"All dharmas are already liberated, for they are fundamentally without attachment. Nāgaśrī spoke again: "O Mañjuśrī!"
"All that can be said regarding their essential words is merely the teaching of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Niu-shou (Nāgasena) again addressed Long-shou (Nāgaśrī), saying:
"As for this Dharma-realm, there is neither speaking nor non-speaking; it has no verbal direction, and it is neither contracted nor extended."
Why is this so? Thus it is, Nāgaśīrṣa!
The dharma-realm is non-existent; that which speaks does not speak, nor is there anything spoken; there is no discursive activity, no attachment, and no conjunction.
He has no conceptualization and no thought; there is nothing that arises for him, nor is there any activity of cessation.
O Dragon Chief, it is like the realm of space:
without conceptualization, without thought, without arising, and without cessation.
All phenomena are likewise; they are identical to empty space. Their fundamental nature is empty, fundamentally unobtainable, and unknowable. Such being their characteristic, it too is unobtainable.
If one were able to apprehend their characteristics, then those Tathāgatas who have entered parinirvāṇa could likewise be apprehended.
It is thus, O Dragon Head!
All dharmas are entirely without location; they are without color, without form, and cannot be seen.

For this reason, although Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have entered parinirvāṇa, within the Dharma there is likewise no one who enters parinirvāṇa; nor is there anyone who enters parinirvāṇa through the elements of earth, water, fire, or wind; nor is there anyone who enters parinirvāṇa through the element of space, nor through the element of consciousness.
Nirvāṇa is like this: even within nirvāṇa there is no nirvāṇa.
If there were the notion of nirvāṇa regarding any phenomena, would there then be the notion of nirvāṇa regarding the realm of empty space?
Why is this? Because all phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally fixed and empty; all phenomena are tranquil, and yet they are further stilled within this.

When those of the class of ordinary, inferior persons give rise to the conceptualization of existence and *nirvāṇa*, they consequently fall into the notion of "self," saying: "I have sensations," "I have a self that experiences," "I have sensations of a life-span," or "I have sensations of a person."

Those who possess conceptual perception and consciousness, yet together with these come to understand that phenomena are ultimately non-existent, immediately give rise to this very perception and conceive of nirvāṇa; for this reason, they fail to attain liberation and are subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death.
To speak briefly, the twelve links of dependent origination culminate in the convergence of great suffering and manifold afflictions; it is for their sake that Nirvāṇa is spoken of.
This is because those who practice with dualistic conceptions do not understand that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, and thus they remain ignorant and fail to awaken.

They act in opposition to the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the Bodhisattvas who possess clear understanding and have deeply entered into skillful means—those who have long planted various roots of goodness and established themselves in non-retrogression, who have accumulated merit and possess great majestic power, and who serve as supreme guides and unsurpassed Great Teachers—and they give rise to contentious thoughts toward such Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, they conflict with the assemblies of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, giving rise to anger and strife against them.
Because of disputing with them, one shall incur great transgression; because of such disputes, one will flow long through birth and death, destined for impure and utterly foul places!
These are forever not praised by any of the holy sages and are to be shunned by all those of supreme wisdom and insight.

For example, noble son, suppose there were a city or a village, not far from which was a place where a great deal of foul filth had accumulated; people would go to that place day and night without ceasing, thereby increasing the impurities, the foul-smelling places, and the unclean things therein.

All foolish, ordinary beings dwell within the five realms of existence; their arising and ceasing never reach an end, and their manifold perceptions remain unsevered, thereby expanding their cycle of birth and death, just like that increasing stench.

Because they lack clarity and do not understand, failing to comprehend the source and failing to realize fundamental non-existence, and because they are shrouded by mists and thick with the darkness of delusion, they undergo extensive transmigration, increasing the flow of birth and death through the five realms. Whether born in hell, or as hungry ghosts, or returning to the animal realm, or as gods or humans, their spiritual transformations are impermanent. They endure the diligent suffering of the five realms, with calamities, perversions, and the piercing pain of wounds—the source of all afflictions and the origin of all miseries—whereby they further increase their foul impurities and emit impure vapors.
It causes those wise and noble sages to regard it as extinction, yet it is that which all greedily crave.

Furthermore, it is what the wise seekers should distance themselves from; through these various defilements, they remain long in bondage and fail to attain liberation. It causes such beings to follow the course of rebirth, returning to existence where there is old age, birth, and the extreme suffering of aging, with myriads of forms of anxiety and distress, leading ultimately to illness and death.
Calamity and fortune follow one; if one is virtuous, there is honor and joy, but if one commits transgressions, disaster ensues.

To state it briefly: when afflictions and transformations gather with fierce intensity, reaching the point where piercing heat and manifold sufferings converge, one consequently fails to escape birth and death.
"However, because they do not realize that its essence is fundamentally non-existent, they undergo birth and death for a long time, just as a foul odor increases.
Nāgaśrī spoke again to Śrīgarbha: "How is it so, Śrīgarbha?"
"How does one attain its root? He replied:
"By means of a mind free from conceptual thought, by means of practice in stillness, and by means of giving rise to tranquil concentration, one proceeds toward entry into purity."
"One who abides in this understands its source.
[The other] asked:
"How so, O Soft-Headed One (Mṛdusa)!?"
"What is meant by the 'solitude of illusion'? He replied:
"One who thoroughly understands that which is like an illusion—this is the solitude and purity of illusion."
At that time, the elder Subhūti went to where Mañjuśrī was and, seeing the great assembly, asked him:
"Noble sirs, you have all gathered here; for what purpose is this discourse being given?"
He replied: "Venerable sir! Regarding all speech, I have said nothing at all."
Furthermore, worthy one!
Have you ever heard of illusory beings having anything to say?
Do echoes in the mountains, dreams, reflections, or mirages engage in conversation?
Have you not heard others say this? Furthermore, worthy one!
Does that which is emanated by the Tathāgata possess ears or sounds?
"Furthermore, is there anyone who hears it?
Is there anyone who recognizes it, or who receives, upholds, and articulates its words, names, and phrases? He replied:
"No," [he replied].
At that moment, Subhūti, while still seated, suddenly entered a state of tranquil extinction amidst a state of dazed oblivion.

Then Śāriputra went to where Rāhula was; seeing that the great assembly was composed mostly of bodhisattvas all listening to the discourse taught by Rāhula, and observing Subhūti sitting there in a state of tranquil extinction, he asked Rāhula:
"For what purpose does this worthy one dwell here in this very state of cessation?
He replied, "Śāriputra!"
This Subhūti is free from contention with any dharma because he has transcended the meditative absorption of cessation. Thus, worthy one!
By means of this practice of non-contention, he is without abiding, without attachment, without nesting, and without dwelling; having passed beyond all cavern-like dharmas, he is in samādhi.
