Then Subhūti entered this meditative absorption, and arising from that concentration, he approached the World-Honored One. He bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, knelt down, and spoke these words:

“I take refuge in all Buddhas, the unsurpassed awakened ones, who have manifested and expounded such profound and subtle images of the Dharma—texts difficult to perceive, beyond the reach of thought or speech, having severed all attachments, being equanimous and free from all conceptualizations, and having attained tranquil peace.”
"How joyful it would be for those non-retrogressive Great Beings and the bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds to hear such an exhortation!
Mañjuśrī then said to Subhūti:
"In this Dharma, there is no speaking, no exhorting, and no object toward which one is directed."
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are without exhortation and without teaching, without discourse and without cognition.

Furthermore, this essential meaning is without speech and without words, without abiding and without movement, without going and without coming, without sitting and without lying down, without leaning and without location, and is moreover nothing at all.
"Why is this? Because these dharmas are fundamentally empty and non-existent; their fundamental nature cannot be apprehended. He said:
"What, O Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī), is meant by 'the dharma of its fundamental practice'?
He replied:
"O worthy one! The non-practice of all dharmas is the essence of practice; one should practice in this way, for to understand this practice is to have reached the ultimate practice."
"If it is so, we may go together on our rounds to seek food.
[The other] said, "Niu-shou!"
I shall no longer enter villages for alms. Why is this?
Because I have attained the hearing of this essential teaching; I am already detached from the village, detached from the perception of a city, and detached from the perception of form.
"To summarize, one is likewise free from perceptions of sound, fragrance, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena; being entirely free from all perceptions, one is without conceptualization.
[Subhūti] said: "Yes, Subhūti!"
"For one who practices by thus departing from these perceptions, how does one proceed or halt?
O Śāradvatīputra, what do you say?
What are the form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are emanated by the Tathāgata?"
By means of which consciousness does the Tathāgata manifest transformations?
By what perceptions do these transformations move forward or stop, look about, or bend and extend their limbs?
He said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
"As the World-Honored One has praised, you are the most enlightened among those who practice in empty, secluded places.
Mañjuśrī spoke again: "Indeed, Subhūti!"
"We should go together to the Buddha to pay our respects, serve him, and make offerings.
Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī) replied again: "Yes, worthy one!"
"I invite you, O Benevolent One, with pure food.
Then Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī:
"Where will you provide us with food?"
"What kind of food should be prepared for him?
He replied, "Indeed, worthy one!"
That which is consumed is neither truly food, nor is it swallowed as food.
Furthermore, that which is swallowed is neither form nor sound, nor is it fragrance or flavor, nor is it texture or smoothness.

The place where they partake of food is not in the realm of desire, nor in the realm of form, nor in the formless realm; it does not abide within the three realms, yet it is not apart from them—this is the place where the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, take their meal.
Then Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī, “Excellent, excellent!
By what you have spoken, I am already fully satisfied.”
"At that time, even the name of this unsurpassed food was praised; how much more so for those who have already eaten such food?
He replied, "Indeed, worthy one!"
That food is not seen by the internal or external eyes, nor is it seen by the divine eye or the wisdom-eye in any location.
When food is taken in such a manner, it is truly a meal of equality.

At that time, the elder Subhūti, Śāriputra, and all the sentient beings, having heard this discourse on the praise of food, immediately entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) right there.
Then, Subhūticitta said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"With what food shall one feed Subhūti, Śāriputra, and the others?
By means of what food do they attain samādhi?"
He replied:
"One practices with the food of the outflows-free (*anāsrava*), practices with the food of non-attachment, and practices with the food of non-aggregation;
one proceeds by means of these practices. One who prepares this food no longer consumes the food of the three realms."
At that time, the venerable Subhūti and Śāriputra arose from their meditative absorption on cessation and each went out to beg for alms.
Then, Subhūti entered the house of a great householder to beg for alms; the householder’s wife was a laywoman (*upāsikā*), and seeing Subhūti standing there in silence, she said to him:
“Venerable sir!...”
"Where are you going?
She replied, "Sister!..."
"I have come to seek alms.
He said, "Virtuous one!"
"Venerable One, have you not yet finished your thoughts regarding the alms-round?
She replied, "Sister!"
"Since the very beginning, I have already fully understood the notion of alms-seeking.
Subhūti said: "O [World-Honored One]!"
"Does that original limit (pūrvakoṭi) have anything that is understood or not understood?
Can one say that from the original limit, the perception of seeking alms has already been understood? He replied:
“Sister! Just as the beginning limit is empty, so too is the end limit empty; all are empty just as the beginning is. The upāsikā said:
"If it is so, worthy one!
Since you have already realized that all things are empty, why do you still speak of what is understood and what is not?
You may simply extend your hand; I shall bestow upon you my portion of alms."
Subhūti then reached out his own hand and said,
“Venerable sir!
"Is this not the hand of an Arhat who, failing to understand its fundamental nature, instead takes the realization of extinction as his goal?
Subhūti said, "Sister!"
The hand of an Arhat has no form; it cannot be seen, nor can it be bent or extended.
It is like a conjured being saying these words to another conjured being:
"What is this so-called 'hand' of a conjurer?"
He spoke again, saying:
"May the hand of the illusionist be extended? He replied:
"Sister! Can this illusory hand be seen?
And can it also be extended?"
He replied, "No. Subhūti said:
"If this is so, sister!
The World-Honored One has taught that all dharmas are like illusions and are fundamentally empty.
"If this is so, worthy one!"
“The World-Honored One has taught that all things are empty; why then, Venerable One, do you continue to seek food?
At that time, the laywoman did not yet give alms to Subhūti, but spoke again:
“Venerable One!”
"You may extend your alms-bowl.
Just as he was about to extend it, the bowl suddenly vanished.
At that time, the upāsikā reached for the bowl with her hand, but the bowl was nowhere to be found, nor did her hand come near Subhūti.
The upāsikā said: “Excellent, excellent!
This is indeed a body of non-attachment and purity, one that the Buddha has praised as that of a practitioner dwelling in seclusion.”
As soon as the upāsikā had spoken these words, the bowl appeared of its own accord.
Then Subhūti stepped forward to receive the bowl; the upāsikā took the bowl, filled it completely with rice, and handed it to Subhūti, saying to him:
"Worthy one!..."
"Is this not the bowl praised by Śākyamuni Buddha as the foremost among those who dwell in seclusion?
She replied: "Sister!"
"As the Buddha has taught, one who practices in seclusion does not possess a bowl.
He replied, "It is so, worthy sir!"
“Does one who practices in seclusion not possess an alms bowl?
She replied, “Sister!”
"There is none.
He said: "Furthermore, O worthy one!"
"When living in seclusion, one does not even possess an alms-bowl; how could there possibly be any further occasion for receiving food?
He replied, "Virtuous One!..."
Since you have already declared yourself one who dwells in seclusion, would there not also be Arhats who attain the realization of Parinirvāṇa?
Furthermore, O worthy one!

Having eaten this food, you should understand that the eater is like an illusion and the food is like a transformation; it is like a person created by transformation eating an illusory meal, or like using a mirage to quench the thirst of one who is parched.
One should understand that the eating of food is exactly like this.
One who clearly understands this accords with the Tathāgata; having realized the root of the three periods of time, there is no longer any need for the practice of begging for alms.
If, worthy one, one gives rise to the thought of giving and perceives a recipient, one thereby creates the constituent factors of existence (*bhava*).

Once these factors of existence are accepted, there arise two views; because of these two views, one returns to the same destination as ordinary worldlings who transmigrate through the five realms of birth and death.
Then the upāsikā spoke again to Subhūti: "Furthermore, worthy one!

Regarding the essential dharma of all Buddhas, it is not only the recipient of food and the donor who should understand that [the gift] is like an illusion and like a magical transformation—fundamentally non-existent and non-occurrent."

As for the phenomena of birth and death and nirvana, one should likewise understand them to be like a dream, an illusion, a transformation, a mirage, a shadow, or an echo, and that they are fundamentally non-existent.

All phenomena should likewise be understood in this way: all phenomena are pure and utterly non-existent; there is no giving and no receiving, no precept and no transgression, no patience and no contention, no diligence and no laziness, no concentration and no distraction, and no wisdom and no folly.
Since all dharmas are entirely non-existent, this practice is what accords with the World-Honored One’s receiving food in accordance with the Dharma.

When a disciple practices the Dharma in this way, understanding the practice of begging for alms (*piṇḍapāta*) as such, they will have no notion of "mixed food" within the triple world, nor will they dwell in the bliss of *nirvāṇa*.
Having heard what the upāsikā had said, Subhūti was immediately bewildered and did not know what to say.
He said, "O noble lady!..."
"Is Nirvana quiescence?
Or is it that there are words for which one simply does not respond? He replied:
"Sister! What words are these that you speak so? Subhūti said, "Sister!"
"Have you realized the nature of illusion? He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"I have realized that all dharmas are entirely like illusions and transformations; both the illusionist and the transformation are fundamentally non-existent and have no reality.

At that moment, Subhūti suddenly emerged from meditative absorption where he sat, wishing to know which vehicle the upāsikā sought as her realization, for her eloquence was so courageous, she dared to utter the lion’s roar, clearly understanding the nature of illusions, and her speech was spontaneous and unimpeded.
Exerting all his effort to observe her state, he saw that the upāsikā was an anāgāmin.
He asked, "Sister!
Have you already attained the stage of anāgāmin?"
The upāsikā said: "How is this, worthy one?
In the fundamental nature of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, could there possibly be the practice of the dharma of an anāgāmin?"

Furthermore, worthy one! The Dharma is formless and colorless; it leaves no trace of coming or conceptualization. It is devoid of the consciousness of "this" and "that," and there is no intermediate activity. It is beyond all that can be conceived, without grasping or realization, and has no location; this alone constitutes the practice of the path of clear understanding.
He said to the worthy one:
"Where is it that the Anāgāmin has completed his task and delights in the realization of the Dharma of Arhatship?
Furthermore, worthy one!

The Dharma has no coming or going; yet that which has coming and going, that which has a destination, that which has an object of pursuit, and that which involves arising, ceasing, recollection, and conceptualization—all these fall within the cycle of transmigration of ordinary beings and have not yet transcended the realm of calculation.

At that time, the upāsikā suddenly, in her own place before Subhūti, manifested a high and wide throne for a great person, adorned with a jeweled canopy, universally displaying a moving and radiant appearance. She clearly turned the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma of *avaivartika*, so that throughout the realm of Śrāvastī and across the lands of the ten directions, there was none who did not hear or see this arising of miraculous transformation.
At that time, twelve thousand devas in the air, having heard what was said, all attained the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).

Within the city of Śrāvastī, twenty-eight thousand people who were dedicated to the practice of the bodhisattva path, by virtue of their accumulated merits from former lives, all attained the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika).

When the multitudes from the ten directions and the great beings who had come heard this teaching, ten billion bodhisattvas—who had previously attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena—upon hearing this supreme and essential exposition, immediately all reached the stage of being born only once more before attaining Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha).

Thereupon, Rāṣṭrapāla and Nāgapāla Bodhisattvas, together with the assembly gathered from all lands, as well as Śāriputra, Subhūti, and the others, having just departed from the city gates of Śrāvastī, suddenly leaped up and ascended into the void.

Bodhisattva Śrīmitra immediately radiated light from his body; its majestic power was brilliant and its splendor magnificent, its luminous reflection dazzling and surpassing that of the sun and moon. It eclipsed all other lights, shining with such pure brilliance as to penetrate even the deepest darkness, like the king of golden-winged birds soaring through the air, such that there were no sentient beings who did not behold it.

As he passed through, all those devas and humans heard these profound and metaphorical discourses on the essential teaching that all phenomena are like dreams, illusions, transformations, mirages, shadows, echoes, bubbles, and plantain trunks; each harbored joy and looked upon one another with a heart of loving-kindness.
All devas and humans hear only the sounds of dreams and illusions; yet this illusory dharma of transformation cannot be apprehended as either seen or unseen.
Those who hear this subtle and wondrous teaching shall gather in assemblies of hundreds of thousands and attain the stage of non-retrogression.

During the time he was traveling through that region, there was the son of a householder named Bhadramati, who had established the roots of virtue in past lives. Having heard the unsurpassed discourse on the essential nature of illusion by Mañjuśrī, and having further witnessed his divine manifestations and transformations, he immediately resolved his mind upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). He then made this vow:
"In a future life, when I attain the state of a Tathāgata, the unsurpassed, equal, and most correct awakening, the manifestations and spiritual stirrings I display shall likewise be such as these."

Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī), seeing that this son of good family possessed the resolute capacity for attaining the sublime and the quality of being precociously intelligent, desired to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas; he thus conceived a great resolve, his mind fixed on the Bodhisattva path and his mouth chanting vows. His voice resonated throughout all quarters like the roar of a lion, and he immediately requested Shan-yi (Kalyāṇamati) and addressed him, saying:
"Son of good family!..."

If you understand that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, you will surely leave behind the weary vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; you shall then attain the aspiration for the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and further come to clearly comprehend the wondrous teaching that all phenomena are like dreams and illusions, being entirely non-existent.
Then the son of the elder knelt and replied, "I have received your explanation that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations.
Mañjuśrī again exhorted the son of the elder with essential words regarding all phenomena; the son of the elder’s heart was filled with joy, and he leaped for gladness.

At that time, the mind of that noble family was vast and expansive; they attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), and eight thousand devas and humans resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Then, five thousand sons of gods dwelling in the void, hearing Mañjuśrī’s discourse on exhortation, were suddenly enlightened in their understanding and attained the patience of the joy of the Dharma of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
All were filled with the utmost solemnity and reverence; having paid homage to Niu-shou (Nāgasena), they suddenly ascended into the void and each returned to their own native lands.

At that time, Niu-shou Bodhisattva, Long-shou Bodhisattva, Śāriputra, Subhūti, and the others returned to the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada. They all approached the World-Honored One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Bodhisattva Nāgaśīrṣa then rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and fully reported to the World-Honored One all the essential teachings on the Dharma that the youth Mañjuśrī had expounded.
Then the Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent,
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta!"

To skillfully expound all phenomena as unsurpassed and subtle—like a dream, like an illusion, like a transformation, like a mirage, a shadow, or an echo—is the ultimate profundity of all wisdom; it is the essential core of all Buddhas.
"This is indeed as it should be: formless, imageless, fundamentally non-existent, and beyond the discourse of illusion.
At that time, the Buddha looked toward the worthy Ānanda and said:
"Receive these essential texts on all dharmas from Mañjuśrī."
Ānanda respectfully approached, knelt down, and said to the Buddha:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
I shall receive it as you have instructed.”
"What shall this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?

At that time, the Buddha again further expounded upon the essential wisdom taught by Niu-shou (Mañjuśrī), Miaoxin (Suvicintita-mati) Bodhisattva, and others; as well as the manifestations and inspirations shown by the laywomen of the Śrāvastī elders to Subhūti, up to the turning of the wheel of the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
The Buddha again addressed Ānanda:
"You should receive this supreme and essential wisdom.
Furthermore, worthy one!"
This is titled *The Sūtra on the Unsurpassed Pure Alms-Gathering of Mañjuśrī*, and it is also titled *The Samādhi that Resolves All Dharmas as Being Like Illusions and Transformations*.
You should diligently remember, receive, and uphold it, and widely proclaim, disseminate, and expound it everywhere.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
If good men and good women, upon hearing this essential teaching, direct their whole hearts toward it with faith—these, Ānanda!
are [the ones who truly understand].
Then one shall behold the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, face to face;
furthermore, one will surely be moved by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and shall eventually achieve the state of a supreme Buddha.
How much more so for those who receive, uphold, recite, study, chant, and practice it accordingly—their merit shall be unsurpassed.

Such sons and daughters of good family will attain the treasury of wisdom of all Buddhas, obtain the supreme and essential seal of all Buddhas, be protected by all Buddhas, and be universally granted the prediction of enlightenment by all the present Buddhas of the ten directions.
"All Buddhas shall personally bestow upon them the prophecy that they shall attain the wisdom of the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Nāgaśiras, Suvicintita, and the other bodhisattvas; Śāriputra, Subhūti, and the assembly of bhikṣus; and all those present in the gathering—gods, nāgas, asuras, humans, and non-humans—heard what the Buddha had said and were all filled with joy. They came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
